extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of science, graduate students, and scholars interested in evolutionary approaches to scientific inquiry
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging or constructing analogies that map evolutionary theory onto the process of scientific inquiry, aimed at producing genuinely explanatory and generative accounts rather than mere re-descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of an analogy = enables further understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of an analogy lies in whether and how it enables further understanding—and analogies are not created equal in this respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An analogy must lead to insights about the target domain (science) that we would not otherwise have; mere resemblance or correct mapping is insufficient. It should be judged by its epistemic payoff: does it help us understand, ask, or solve new questions about the target?

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide an intuitively appealing organizing structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A really good analogy ... will provide a structure for thinking about a topic that is intuitively appealing and will make the significance of certain questions obvious and relatively easy to articulate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good analogies offer a clear conceptual frame (example: Darwin’s selective-breeding analogy) that helps practitioners identify leading questions and directions for inquiry. Evaluate whether the analogy produces such an organizing framework and whether it resonates with users' existing background knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generate leading questions and suggest ways to answer them
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of such analogies ... has always resided in what they offer researchers by way of organizing a domain of phenomena, generating new questions, and suggesting how to begin answering them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the analogy supplies concrete research questions and plausible methodological starting points rather than only descriptive parallels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight potential mismatches between source and target
rubrics_metrics.description: Another part of the analogy’s strength lies in its ability to highlight potential mismatches, such as whether the difference between breeder’s intentional action and the purely physical operation of nature is meaningful enough to constitute a difference in mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A fruitful analogy should expose where the comparison breaks down and make those limits informative, not merely hide mismatches. Use mismatches to refine questions and identify boundaries of applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must indicate significant philosophical problems and how to approach them
rubrics_metrics.description: It must provide us at least with a sense of what some of the significant philosophical problems are, and of roughly how to approach those problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies need not solve philosophical puzzles outright but should reveal which phenomena deserve explanation and propose plausible approaches for tackling them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not merely accurate mapping; be generative rather than only descriptive
rubrics_metrics.description: There is more to a fruitful analogy than mere accuracy, and understanding what has prevented previous versions of the analogy from bearing fruit will give us some purchase on what form the analogy might need to take.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid analogies that are technically accurate but uninformative. Prioritize analogies that produce new explanatory leverage or research trajectories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage contemporary developments in evolutionary theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Previous attempts did not have the benefit of recent progress: substantial gains in clarity, detail, structure, and scope associated with central concepts in evolutionary biology over the past four decades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful analogy should incorporate modern evolutionary concepts (e.g., refined notion of Darwinian populations, ecological speciation, niche construction, mass extinction) rather than relying on outdated or oversimplified evolutionary ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embed sociocultural features of scientific practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Much of the evolutionary analogy’s ability to shed light on the philosophical problems surrounding scientific knowledge depends on recognizing the significant influence of sociocultural factors in science—science is a social process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analogy must account for communal and social structures (norms, institutions, credit economies, training) that shape variation, selection, and transmission in science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use evolutionary theory to explain (not just describe) epistemic phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: None of the previous attempts ... employs evolutionary theory as a framework for solving philosophical puzzles associated with scientific knowledge. Nothing about science is depicted as strange or in need of explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the analogy provides explanatory claims about why scientific phenomena occur (e.g., why science tends to produce progressive change) rather than merely re-describing them in evolutionary language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid narrow focus on competitive exclusion/selection alone
rubrics_metrics.description: The exclusive focus on competitive exclusion as the mechanism of selection occludes the interesting panoply of selective influences that can bear on members of a population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A robust analogy should incorporate multiple forms of selective influence (cooperation, cultural selection, environmental filtering, institutional pressures), not reduce the model to winner-take-all competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow for nonrandom (directed) variation, not only blind variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Blind variation is really just a limiting case in the theory of natural selection; natural selection can still operate in contexts where there is a nonrandom association between the demands of the environment and the properties of variants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies should recognize that variation in scientific practice can be biased or structured (e.g., guided by heuristics, theory-driven exploration) and model how such nonrandom variation interacts with selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify mechanisms of inheritance, transmission, and replication
rubrics_metrics.description: Hull’s account emphasizes the importance of inheritance mechanisms in science ... replicators (elements of substantive content) and interactors (books, journals, scientists) play key roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A credible evolutionary analogy must identify what is transmitted (replicators), how transmission occurs (interactors/media), and how persistence/change of content is effected in scientific communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use representative empirical cases and avoid idiosyncratic examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Hull’s focus on development of systematics as a case study is a highly nonrepresentative case ... the excesses of the systematics wars are in no way characteristic of the social dynamics of science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test analogical claims on a range of typical scientific contexts rather than extrapolating from anomalous or extreme episodes; ensure empirical plausibility and generalizability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid shoehorning or misleading distortions of practice
rubrics_metrics.description: If we are motivated to make the analogy work, we are likely to be prone—as was Campbell—to misleading distortions in our representation of scientific practice (Godfrey-Smith’s 'shoehorning').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware forcing the target to fit the source domain; maintain fidelity to the actual practices and causal mechanisms of science when mapping evolutionary concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for group-level social phenomena (isolation, deme dynamics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chief among these is the tendency of small groups of practitioners to effectively isolate themselves from other groups ... as they slowly progress toward a satisfactory understanding of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analogy should explain how small-group isolation, deme structure, and inter-group interactions shape variation, testing, and retention in science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose why science succeeds relative to other cultural processes
rubrics_metrics.description: I argue that ... science often functions as a Darwinian population. The differences between science and other cultural processes are ... because the sciences tend to more closely approximate Darwinian populations than do other groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong analogy should help explain the distinctive epistemic success of science (its capacity for progressive improvement) by showing structurally how scientific communities achieve Darwinian-like dynamics more effectively than other cultural practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make an explanatory contribution to accounts of epistemic rationality
rubrics_metrics.description: Toulmin goes to considerable lengths to answer the philosophical demand to give an account of how the norms governing acceptable inferences can be fixed by local context while doing (some) justice to traditional notions of epistemic rationality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies should be able to inform debates about rationality in science—showing how local epistemic norms, social context, and evolutionary dynamics can be reconciled with broader notions of epistemic improvement.
